newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African mutual funds prepare for offshore demand.
newsitem.headline: S.African mutual funds prepare for offshore demand.

text.p: South African mutual funds anticipate strong demand for offshore investments under a newly-relaxed foreign exchange control regime.

Association of Unit Trusts executive officer Colin Woodin told Reuters that mutual fund investments offshore could more than double to 4.4 billion rand as a result of concessions announced this month by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel.
Manuel bowed to market pressure for a further relaxation of exchange controls affecting residents in his March 12 budget.
The budget moves favoured individuals, including proposed legalisation on personal foreign currency holdings.

But for the burgeoning mutual funds industry, there was one key concession -- institutions were given the go ahead to invest up to 10 percent of their total assets abroad and not, as before, 10 percent of each individual mutual fund.

Woodin said the concession, for which the central Reserve Bank quickly gave the go ahead, would facilitate the foreign investment of up to 10 percent of the industry's December 1996 asset base of 43.8 billion rand.
"The exciting thing is that it opens up a whole new class of investment -- the truly international fund. I think it will give the industry a tremendous boost," he said.

Existing "global" or "international" funds operated by the country's major investment houses include up to 10 percent in foreign holdings with the rest invested in rand hedge shares -- local companies with strong foreign exchange income streams.

Manuel extended a 1996 concession allowing the institutions to directly invest three percent of the previous year's net capital inflow abroad, freeing up around 220 million rand for investment in 1997.
But in a measure to protect reserves, he said remaining investments under the 10 percent rule would still have to be in the form of asset swaps with foreign partners.

Old Mutual, the country's biggest investment group, planned to raise the offshore component of its Global Equity Fund from the current 10 percent to 95 percent as soon as possible, said marketing manager Di Turpin.
"We expect a flood of money to come in specifically as a result of the fact that the unit trust industry can officially now go offshore," she said.
She said this global fund would shed most of its local rand hedge holdings, but the firm would not bring into it offshore investments placed in other funds.
Old Mutual manages 9.7 billion rand in mutual funds, known locally as unit trusts, and has so far invested less than 460 million rand of its 970 million rand ceiling abroad.
More than 400 million of that offshore investment is held by the corporation's flagship Investors Fund. The 600 million rand Global Equity Fund is already at its 10 percent limit.
"We do have a large, a very large swap pending at the moment. Once that's through, the first money will definitely go into the international fund.
"We fully expect to take the Global Equity Fund up to 95 percent," she said.
South African mutual fund rules require all funds to keep five percent of their assets in local cash to meet withdrawal requirements.
Sanlam Unit Trusts managing director Charl le Roux said his group had placed all its offshore investments into its 130 million rand Global Trust.
But he said the group was negotiating asset swaps that could massively increase its offshore mutual fund investment of under 13 million rand.
With potential to invest up to 450 million rand abroad, le Roux said Sanlam would "be looking at different investment opportunities abroad most urgently".
He anticipated that Sanlam's Global Trust could grow by 300 to 400 percent in the short term.
